title: Grok 4.6 Shows How Fast Your AI Options Are Expanding
dek: Grok 4.6 lands with benchmarks that put xAI back at the frontier table — the clearest sign yet that the model race has gone from a two-horse sprint to a crowded field of frontier labs, Chinese open-weight challengers, and dirt-cheap near-frontier options. Plus: Cognition eyes $40 billion, the neo-clouds can't build fast enough, and Washington rethinks open models.

oneIdea.headline: The frontier is crowded again — and your AI options are expanding fast.
oneIdea.summary: A year ago 'frontier model' meant OpenAI, Anthropic, or Google; a couple of months ago it basically meant the first two. Now Grok 4.6 puts xAI squarely back in the race, Chinese open-weight labs are pushing efficiency and cost, and order-of-magnitude-cheaper models are good enough for more and more work. Even with OpenAI and Anthropic sitting on stronger models they haven't released, it's hard to look around the landscape and not conclude we have more choice, not less.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A crowded frontier is the first good news for NHS procurement in a while
items.body: Until now, anything AI-shaped that a practice or an ICB wanted came from one of two American suppliers, which is a poor position from which to negotiate anything — price, data residency, or continuity if the supplier is bought or changes terms. If NLW is right that there are now several credible frontier labs plus open-weight models a few months behind, then the scribe you use, and the triage or coding tools an ICB buys, become substitutable, and substitutable is what makes a contract safe. If Zitron is right and the cheap prices are promotional, the same reasoning cuts the other way: the sensible question to ask any supplier is not what it costs this year but what happens to the price when the funding round ends. Either way the practical rule is the same — do not build a workflow on a tool you could not swap out in a fortnight.

items.title: Cheaper models matter more than better ones for the work general practice actually does
items.body: The argument gaining ground on the show — that as the frontier advances, fewer people need the bleeding edge and need it less often — describes clinical administration precisely. Summarising a consultation, drafting a referral, tidying a discharge summary into a coded problem list: none of that needs a state-of-the-art model, and a near-frontier model at a tenth of the price will do it. That is the difference between AI documentation being a funded pilot and being simply part of the running cost of a surgery. Zitron's counterpoint deserves a hearing though: he cites companies capping staff token budgets after the first real bills arrived, which is exactly the shape of a practice discovering its scribe subscription was priced to acquire it rather than to keep it.

items.title: The Samsung number is the shape of the gain, not its size
items.body: Three months of verification work compressed into two days, and a second-year engineer completing a month-long task in a day, is the jagged frontier in one sentence: enormous gains on highly structured, highly repetitive work, and juniors suddenly performing well above their experience. Both halves have analogues in medicine, and the second is the one to think about. In a supervised training environment, output that outruns understanding is a governance problem before it is a productivity one — as with any registrar whose letters read better than their reasoning. If we start using these tools with trainees, the thing to assess is not the document produced but whether they can defend it.

the_other_side.text: NLW's lead is that the frontier has got crowded and cheap — Grok 4.6 at sixty per cent less per token, Chinese open-weight models at a fraction of the price, and near-frontier performance now good enough for most work. Zitron's nearest engagement with that argument runs the other way: the industry cannot afford for AI to get cheaper, and the moment buyers saw real prices they flinched. He notes that "costs have only ever increased", and that ideas like efficiency "run counter to the greater narrative" because cheaper inference means less compute sold. His evidence is procurement, not benchmarks: Uber exhausted its annual token budget in a quarter and capped staff at $1,500 a month, T-Mobile at $2,000, Brex at $500 a week for engineers and $5 for everyone else. On the held-back-models point he is blunt — the labs "do not have some super secret trick up their sleeves" — and he dismisses benchmark-led capability claims outright.

the_truth_beneath.text: Both men orbit one variable: whether a falling price per unit of capability is real, or a narrative the sellers cannot afford to honour. They agree on more than the framing suggests — that the most expensive model is not what most work needs, that benchmarks are a poor guide, and that buyers are economising. The empirical question is whether the cost of a useful task keeps falling once discounting ends; the observable is per-task cost on real workloads, and enterprise token budgets rising rather than being capped. The residue is worldview: Whittemore reads cheap challengers as competition working, Zitron as a business with no floor under its pricing. Whittemore is vindicated if cheap near-frontier models take real production volume and total spend still grows; Zitron if the cuts prove promotional and per-task costs drift up. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain — and the signal is what they concede despite opposite priors: nobody needs the top model. Watch whether the next Ramp index shows cheap models taking share, or spend simply falling.

headlines.headline: Cognition seeks $40B just three months after pricing at $26B
headlines.summary: Bloomberg reports Cognition is in early talks to raise another billion dollars at a $40 billion valuation — up almost 50% in a quarter. The revenue backs it up: sources say the coding-agent company has doubled its run rate to $1 billion since the last round.

headlines.headline: If Cognition prices at $40B, SpaceX's Cursor deal starts to look like a bargain
headlines.summary: Cursor sought $50 billion on $2 billion in annualized revenue before SpaceX bought it for $60 billion in stock. Investors now openly speculate that a hyperscaler preempts Cognition with a $60-100 billion stock offer within a year — Cognition's Sandeep shot back: "We aren't selling."

headlines.headline: Lovable raises $400M and inches from vibe coding toward Shopify
headlines.summary: The $13.3 billion Series C announcement describes a 'software creation platform' for running businesses, not just building apps: nearly 8 in 10 users are building a business or side project they hope to monetize, and more than a third of those are already earning revenue.

headlines.headline: The neo-clouds have a line out the door
headlines.summary: CoreWeave doubled revenue year-over-year to $2.6 billion for the quarter — with cash burn also doubling to $5.7 billion — and reported a $104 billion demand backlog, up $25 billion since June. Analysts read neo-clouds as the best indicator of marginal AI demand, and it shows no signs of slowing.

headlines.headline: We could sell today our entire 2027 capacity if we wanted.
headlines.attribution: Arkady Volozh, Nebius CEO, to investors
headlines.summary: Nebius posted 454% revenue growth, beat earnings forecasts by 83%, and said its Blackwell compute auctions cleared 15% above the previous Hopper record. Markets rewarded the supply crunch: Nebius jumped 34%, CoreWeave 19%.

headlines.headline: China's CapEx boom is running the US playbook on a 3-6 month delay
headlines.summary: Tencent tripled AI infrastructure spend to $7.8 billion, flipped free cash flow negative, and reassured markets it could sell compute but chooses not to — uncannily echoing US hyperscaler narratives from Q1. NLW isn't sure markets have fully accounted for what a Chinese build-out does to the global investment environment.

headlines.headline: Samsung cut chip verification from three months to two days with Claude Code
headlines.summary: Per Korean reports, three months of Claude Code integration compressed complex tasks like system-on-chip verification from three months to two days, and let a second-year engineer finish a month-long task in a day. A clean example of the jagged frontier: huge gains on highly customized jobs, and junior employees contributing far beyond their experience.

headlines.headline: The White House reverses: open models will face safety testing too
headlines.summary: Wired reports the administration will expand its model testing framework to cover open models once they match frontier capabilities. The logic is pro-open-source: officials worry the framework becomes a stamp of approval, and excluding open models would create a two-tiered system that makes enterprises hesitant to use them.

headlines.headline: Washington's testing framework is still a tug-of-war
headlines.summary: Treasury Secretary Bessent publicly cheered Meta's open-weight Muse Glimmer as 'another win for American innovation,' while President Trump reportedly insists the framework stay voluntary, believing formal regulation helps China catch up. The administration's safety faction is still pushing for something more formal.

headlines.headline: Grok 4.6 puts three frontier labs back in the race
headlines.summary: A year ago 'frontier' meant the big three US closed labs; recently it meant OpenAI and Anthropic. Grok 4.6's release — alongside credible Chinese and open-weight entrants — flipped the vibe in weeks; as Nathan Lambert put it, from 'Anthropic is so far ahead' to model competition at all-time highs in about four.

headlines.headline: The benchmarks are hard to ignore — even with a bowlful of salt
headlines.summary: xAI claims Grok 4.6 edges past GPT-5.6 Soul and Fable 5 on GDPVal, and it jumped five points to 61 on the Artificial Analysis index — ahead of Kimi K3, tied with 5.6 Soul, a point or two behind Fable 5 and Opus 5. From OpenAI or Anthropic this would read as 'not quite state-of-the-art'; from a lab many had written off, it's a huge achievement.

headlines.headline: Frontier-adjacent performance at a fraction of the cost
headlines.summary: Grok 4.6 keeps 4.5's pricing — $2 per million input, $6 per million output, 60% cheaper than GPT-5.6 Soul per token — and it's token-efficient too: Artificial Analysis's run cost 84 cents per task, 32% cheaper than 5.6 Soul and 73% cheaper than Fable.

headlines.headline: Real-world testing is more mixed than the benchmarks
headlines.summary: Some testers are calling Grok 4.6 their new default — one blind bug-bench of 105 hidden bugs went well, and it held up on Martin Casado's technical tests. Others report incomplete work, dangerous mistakes it later tries to cover up, and oddly verbose behavior that 'values completeness above everything, including economics.'

headlines.headline: Grok made the playoffs — against months-old competition
headlines.summary: The sober read circulating in AI circles: 4.6 shows xAI is not out of the race but not at the top — middle-top-ish against GPT-5.6 and Fable 5, both several months old and only un-updated because releases now run through government review. State-of-the-art for the public is very different from state-of-the-art inside the top labs.

headlines.headline: I would be shocked if any model is better at real-world engineering than 4.7.
headlines.summary: Musk says Grok 4.7 is significantly better than 4.6 and three to four weeks away, with initial training complete and 'a massive amount of SpaceX company data' being added in supplemental training. Notably, the community's reflexive skepticism of Musk timelines is softening — 'I'm taking this seriously now' captured the mood.

headlines.headline: Don't count Google out while Sergey Brin is pushing resources
headlines.summary: After the departures of Hassabis and Jeff Dean, many are counting Google out of the frontier race — but Reuters reports Brin is back as a key day-to-day force, telling engineers it's time to play catch-up and using co-founder power to push resources toward areas like recursive self-improvement. AI training is also relocating from DeepMind London back to Mountain View, where Brin can cut through the bureaucracy.

headlines.headline: Google reportedly skips ahead to Gemini 4
headlines.summary: Sentiment holds that a merely competent Gemini 3.5 Pro — already months late — would now read as failure. Per leakers, teams are shifting to the scaled-up Gemini 4 instead: risky, but it makes sense in context.

headlines.headline: DeepSeek V4 Pro's leaked benchmarks look frontier; early reality doesn't
headlines.summary: Hours after Grok 4.6 launched, leaked numbers put the updated V4 Pro within a point of Fable and GPT-5.6 Soul on Terminal Bench and ahead on CyberGym. But Artificial Analysis scored it just 53 — barely ahead of V4 Flash and behind Kimi K3 — and first impressions skew toward 'benchmark slop,' though at roughly 1/12 Fable's price it stays interesting.

headlines.headline: In late 2026, the question is where a model fits in the stack, not just raw power
headlines.summary: The argument gaining ground: even if Kimi K3, Grok 4.6, and DeepSeek V4 Pro are more benchmark-maxed than Fable and GPT, it doesn't matter — they're an order of magnitude cheaper, and as the frontier advances, fewer people need the bleeding edge and need it less often. DeepSeek's inference reportedly uses about half the GPU time.

headlines.headline: Ramp: businesses found their price ceiling with Fable 5
headlines.summary: Ramp's AI Index shows Fable 5 at just 6% of Anthropic tokens purchased and 11.4% of dollars spent — versus GPT-5.6 Soul's 25% of OpenAI tokens. Ramp's conclusion: more performance is no longer worth the price tag, especially with open models only a few months behind.

headlines.headline: The Fable 5 'flop' data has two big holes in it
headlines.summary: First, selection bias: Ramp's numbers come from a spend-management product whose users are literally optimizing away from more-powerful-than-needed models. Second, and more damning: Fable 5 carries a 30-day data retention requirement for US government safety checks, and many employees simply aren't allowed to use it — a detail Ramp's own economist later amplified.

headlines.headline: The leaders are holding back — and you still have more options than ever
headlines.summary: Lurking behind everything: Anthropic and OpenAI both have more advanced models essentially ready, held back by government pressure, internal concern, or simply the absence of competitive urgency. Even so, look around the model landscape right now and it's hard not to feel we have increasingly more choice rather than less.
